input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: The project did not actively re-center or frequently narrow because backtests showed the strategy underperformed a passive wide range. While narrowing generated ~4x more fees, the impermanent loss (IL) and re-centering costs (swaps) exceeded those gains. For example, on the 720-day window, passive wide earned $3,280 on cbBTC versus $2,983 for the narrow strategy, despite the narrow one earning $2,169 in fees versus $541. The narrow approach lost because IL consumed roughly $1.9k–$2.9k more than the fee premium, a phenomenon described as "short gamma" where every re-centering realizes divergence. This held true even in flat market regimes where narrowing theoretically should have an advantage.

Wąskie pasmo to short gamma: każde przejście postury REALIZUJE dywergencję.
passive wide range ≈ HODL + fees − a little IL

input.question: Why did we keep the capital commitment small even though ETH and BTC were rising?
input.reference: Tranche 1 ($6 092) was planned as a first stage and run as an operational experiment on a calibration the team itself considered broken (720 d: 0/21), the entry after an ETH +25%/90d pump was recorded with an explicit FOMO note, and on 02.09 the product failed to beat HODL in all five measurements, so the planned scale-up never happened.
input.answer: The project kept capital small because the strategy's edge is modest and asymmetric: in calm markets it beats HODL by only ~$50–100 in fees, but in a crash it loses $500–1,100 more. The core verdict was that "alphy nie ma" (there is no alpha); the product is essentially "HODL+yield−drag". When assets rise, the pool sells the rising asset (impermanent loss), so the LP earns "MNIJ NIEŻ HODL" (less than HODL). The limited upside and high downside risk justified a small tranche size.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: In an uptrend the LP earns less in fees than in a flat market because the price moves out of the provided range, so trading (and thus fee accrual) stops. In a flat market the price stays inside the range, generating continuous swaps. The journal confirms this: "We FLAT wszystko wygrywa" (in flat, all strategies win), while in UP windows the active mechanisms "kosztował więcej, niż dawał" (cost more than they gave), and the narrow range "umiera na IL od trendu" (dies from IL due to trend).

input.question: What infrastructure problems were there, was anything changed on the production machine while the capital was already invested, and when?
input.reference: Before the capital (27.08) there was the .bot/pipeline overwrite incident (17.08), the auto-pull runner withdrawn (18.08) and the NSSM to pm2 migration rolled back (21.08); while the capital was in the LP (27.08 to 18.09) the Windows machine was changed repeatedly: bot and UI deployments with restarts on 28.08, 29.08 (including sigma on the 15-minute grid), 31.08, 01.09, 02.09, 03.09 and 11.09, plus a disk replacement on the night of 02/03.09 that stopped the pipeline, report and observer; known ledger bugs (anchor chain, cost after the 11.09 rebalance) were left unfixed.
input.answer: Yes. On 21 Aug 2026 (before the 27 Aug capital deployment), a deployment script (`deploy/deploy.ps1`) still contained `pm2 startOrReload` + `pm2 save` from a pre-10 Aug era, while production ran on NSSM. An AI session misinterpreted this as a migration, stopped NSSM services, and started pm2, leaving the production machine on pm2. This caused recurring duplicate terminal windows after reboots because every subsequent deploy silently re-enabled pm2 alongside NSSM. The script was rewritten to use NSSM and remove pm2. Additionally, during the live capital period (after 27 Aug), a rebalance transaction reverted due to a stale pool state in the UI, which was fixed and documented the same day.
